question: Prediction of progression from MCI to AD in ADNI MCI participants, from (a) FDG-PET alone and (b) cognitive/clinical scores alone. P-81: 164 sMCI / 93 pMCI, conversion within 3 years. P-88: 341 MCI, 102 progressing during up to 8 years of follow-up. Same task, population class and channels (PET; clinical/cognitive data). Horizon, PET representation (whole-brain 3D CNN vs a 10-feature white-matter radiomics signature) and cognitive predictor set (5-score composite vs single ADAS or CDR) differ, which the rule allows.
metric: ROC-AUC with ROC-AUC on both arms. The record's disputed quantity is the ordering 'cognitive scores vs FDG-PET alone'.

figures.P-81: 5-fold CV, mean +- fold SD (Table 3). PET only: AUC 0.6102 +- 0.0231; CS only: AUC 0.7496 +- 0.0683. The fold SDs are not 95% intervals, so Hanley-McNeil intervals are derived with 93 pMCI / 164 sMCI. PET: Q1 = 0.6102/1.3898 = 0.4391; Q2 = 2*0.6102^2/1.6102 = 0.4625; SE^2 = [0.2379 + 92*(0.4391-0.3723) + 163*(0.4625-0.3723)]/(93*164) = 21.07/15252 = 0.00138; SE = 0.0372; interval [0.537, 0.683]. The interval is [0.531, 0.689] if only 85% of subjects (79/139) entered the CV folds. CS: SE = 0.0331; interval [0.685, 0.815].
figures.P-88: Time-ordered split by ADNI entry number, test group 72 stable / 31 progressive (Table 1). Test AUCs (Table 3): psychoradiomics (white-matter FDG-PET) signature 0.719; ADAS 0.742; CDR 0.737. Training: 0.747 / 0.755 / 0.683. No intervals printed. Hanley-McNeil for PET 0.719 with 31/72: Q1 = 0.5613; Q2 = 0.6015; SE^2 = [0.2020 + 30*(0.5613-0.5170) + 71*(0.6015-0.5170)]/(31*72) = 7.532/2232 = 0.00337; SE = 0.0581; interval [0.605, 0.833]. ADAS 0.742: SE = 0.0566; interval [0.631, 0.853].

matched_figure_check: No matched figure exists. P-88 reports no fixed 3-year result and no whole-brain PET model. P-81 reports no radiomics signature and no longer horizon. On the ordering the record disputes, the printed AUCs agree in direction: P-81 has cognition 0.750 above PET 0.610, and P-88 has ADAS 0.742 and CDR 0.737 above PET 0.719 on the test set (ADAS 0.755 vs PET 0.747 in training). P-88's sentence that the rad-score 'was superior to clinical scale scores' is not borne out by its own Table 3 AUCs and was not tested (DeLong only for the integrated model). The accuracies it prints for the scales (ADAS 0.551 test) cannot be reproduced from its own sensitivity/specificity (0.645/0.75 on 31/72 gives about 0.72). The cognitive arms agree: 0.750 [0.685, 0.815] and 0.742 [0.631, 0.853] lie within each other's intervals.
performance_validity: Neither study meets the exclusion: no conversion AUC reaches 0.97. P-81's 1.0 values are its CN-vs-AD pre-training, which the authors attribute to circularity; they are not part of the conversion comparison.

candidate_explanations.difference: Prediction horizon: conversion within 3 years (P-81) against progression at any time during up to 8 years of follow-up (P-88). P-81's authors name horizon as a factor that affects comparison across studies.
candidate_explanations.quote: One significant factor to take into account is the duration over which the models make predictions.
In total, we enrolled 341 patients with MCI, and 102 of these patients progressed to AD during a follow-up period of 8 years

candidate_explanations.difference: PET representation and model: P-81 feeds the whole-brain FDG-PET image to a 3D CNN first trained to separate AD from controls and then transferred. Table 3 reports the zero-shot predictions. P-88 builds a 10-feature radiomics signature from white-matter PET.
candidate_explanations.quote: Table 3 shows the prediction performance from zero-shot predictions.

candidate_explanations.difference: P-81's transfer from a CN-vs-AD classifier.
candidate_explanations.quote: we first trained a classification 3D-CNN to differentiate between the brains of dementia patients and cognitively normal “healthy control” subjects. Afterward, we performed transfer learning to adapt the task to predicting dementia conversion.

candidate_explanations.difference: Validation design: 5-fold CV (P-81) against a single split by ADNI entry number, with 103 test subjects (P-88).
candidate_explanations.quote: We divided these patients according to their entry numbers in the ADNI database as follows: training group, 238 patients and test group, 103 patients.

reason: The recorded dispute, whether cognition or FDG-PET alone predicts conversion better, dissolves on the printed AUCs: both studies put cognitive scores at or above PET. The cognitive arms agree within uncertainty. What remains is the PET-alone AUC: P-88's test estimate (0.719) lies outside P-81's derived interval [0.537, 0.683]. By the letter of condition 4 that is a qualifying gap, and no matched figure closes it. I mark it borderline, not yes, because the exclusion holds in one direction only: P-81's 0.610 lies inside P-88's interval [0.605, 0.833], and a two-sample comparison gives z = (0.719-0.610)/sqrt(0.0372^2+0.0581^2) = 1.58. The gap also sits on a quantity the ledger record did not dispute. Candidate explanations (horizon, zero-shot transfer from a CN-vs-AD PET model against a white-matter radiomics signature, validation design) are not shown to be sufficient.

quotes.quote: FDG-PET and CS were obtained at MCI diagnosis to predict AD conversion within three years of MCI diagnosis using convolutional neural networks.
including 205 patients with the diagnosis of Dementia of Alzheimer’s type (DAT), 150 cognitively normal subjects, 164 stable-MCI subjects, and 93 unstable-MCI subjects.
also found that the rad-score was superior to clinical scale scores
